ai.definition: Cognitive Process Orchestration is an advanced software technology designed to autonomously manage inter-departmental workflows within organizations, eliminating the need for human intervention.
ai.howItWorks: This system operates through a hierarchy of 'Manager' and 'Worker' agents that negotiate resource allocation in real-time. Managers oversee multiple Worker agents, which execute specific tasks based on predefined rules and dynamic conditions. The negotiation process ensures efficient use of resources and optimizes workflow execution across departments.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the inefficiencies and delays caused by manual intervention in complex supply chains and inter-departmental workflows, thereby improving overall operational efficiency.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing and integrating AI algorithms, creating a robust agent-based architecture, and ensuring secure communication between Manager and Worker agents. This includes training large datasets to enable the agents to make informed decisions autonomously.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with defining the workflow structure and task allocation rules. Then, custom AI models are developed for each role (Manager and Worker). These models undergo extensive testing in simulation environments before deployment. Finally, the system is integrated into existing IT infrastructure and fine-tuned based on real-world performance data.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include initial development costs, continuous training of AI models, maintenance expenses, and integration with legacy systems. The cost can vary widely depending on the complexity of workflows and the extent of customization required.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to see widespread adoption in the near future as more organizations recognize the benefits of automated workflow management, particularly in complex supply chains.
ai.regulation: Regulations will likely focus on data privacy, security, and transparency. Organizations must ensure compliance with existing laws while also preparing for potential new regulations specific to AI-driven automation systems.
ai.risks: Risks include potential job displacement due to reduced human involvement, cybersecurity threats, and the complexity of maintaining an agent-based system. There is also a risk that initial implementation may face challenges in integrating with legacy systems.
ai.profitability: Profitability will depend on the efficiency gains achieved through reduced operational costs and improved supply chain performance. However, the technology's adoption rate could be slow due to concerns about job displacement and cybersecurity.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development is likely to focus on enhancing AI capabilities for better decision-making, improving agent communication protocols, and expanding application areas beyond complex supply chains to other business processes.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Overall operational power consumption is moderate but can vary based on the number of active agents and their computational demands.

glossary.def: A high-level AI entity that oversees multiple Worker agents, making strategic decisions about resource allocation.
Lower-level AI entities responsible for executing specific tasks based on instructions from Manager agents and real-time conditions.
The dynamic interaction between Manager and Worker agents to allocate resources efficiently and ensure smooth workflow execution.

subsystems.name: Process model
subsystems.role: a machine-readable map of the workflow: steps, owners, dependencies, deadlines and exception paths.

subsystems.name: Planning layer
subsystems.role: turns a goal such as 'clear this backlog' into an ordered set of tasks and assigns them.

subsystems.name: Manager agents
subsystems.role: supervise a group of tasks, watch for failure or delay, reallocate and escalate.

subsystems.name: Worker agents
subsystems.role: actually do the work: call an API, update a record, draft a message, request a signature.
parts: robotic process automation for legacy screens

subsystems.name: Negotiation and allocation
subsystems.role: lets agents bid for scarce resources (budget, staff time, dock slots) instead of waiting for a human decision.

subsystems.name: State and audit store
subsystems.role: a durable log of every task, decision and result so the workflow can resume after a crash and be reviewed.

subsystems.name: Guardrails
subsystems.role: limits what agents may do without a person: spending caps, permission scopes, approval gates.

buildSteps.title: Map the process as it really runs
buildSteps.detail: Interview staff and mine existing system logs to recover the true sequence of steps, the common exceptions and where delays actually occur.

buildSteps.title: Make every step callable
buildSteps.detail: Wrap each action — check stock, book a shipment, raise a purchase order — as a typed tool with defined inputs, outputs and failure modes.

buildSteps.title: Define the agent hierarchy
buildSteps.detail: Decide which decisions a worker may take alone, which need a manager agent, and which must go to a person; write these as explicit rules.

buildSteps.title: Build the planner and allocator
buildSteps.detail: Implement goal decomposition plus a bidding or constraint-solving scheme so tasks are assigned against real costs, deadlines and capacities.

buildSteps.title: Add durable state
buildSteps.detail: Put every task and decision into an event log so a workflow can be paused, replayed and resumed without duplicating orders or payments (idempotency).

buildSteps.title: Set permissions and guardrails
buildSteps.detail: Give each agent its own identity with the minimum rights it needs, plus spending caps, rate limits and mandatory approval points.

buildSteps.title: Shadow-run against historical data
buildSteps.detail: Replay months of past cases and compare the agents' proposed decisions with what humans did, before any live action is allowed.

buildSteps.title: Pilot in one department
buildSteps.detail: Run with humans approving each action, measure exceptions and hand-offs, and widen autonomy only where the error rate stays acceptable.

buildSteps.title: Expand across departments
buildSteps.detail: Connect the second and third process so manager agents can negotiate across them, then keep monitoring for drift and new failure modes.

prerequisites.why: agents can only be as dependable as the systems they call; many supply-chain steps still sit behind legacy interfaces.
strong on single steps, still weak at long chains of decisions without losing track or drifting from instructions.
decades of business-process and messaging software already provide restartable, exactly-once execution.
agent-to-agent messaging, capability description and hand-off formats are still being standardised and are not yet interoperable.

prerequisites.tech: Identity, audit and accountability for autonomous actors
prerequisites.why: an organisation must be able to say which agent did what, under whose authority, when a decision is challenged.
there is no settled way to certify that a long-horizon agent workflow is safe and correct before it runs at scale.

pathway.milestone: single-team agent workflows with a person approving each action
pathway.unlocks: automation of repetitive steps and faster exception triage.

pathway.milestone: cross-department orchestration inside one company, with manager agents reallocating work
pathway.unlocks: end-to-end handling of supply disruptions without waiting on meetings.

pathway.milestone: negotiated orchestration between separate firms' agents under contract terms
pathway.unlocks: real-time rerouting of orders and capacity across a supplier network.

pathway.milestone: continuously self-optimising processes bounded by formal rules and full audit
pathway.unlocks: planning that adapts to demand and disruption faster than human review cycles.
